meta.title: Istwa Ayiti — seed dataset
meta.note: Phase 0 seed: ~125 events drafted from general historical knowledge. Every event gets source cross-checking in Phase 1 before public launch. Dates marked c (circa) are approximate.

events.b: Archaic-age peoples settle the island their Taino descendants would call Ayiti — land of mountains. The dates are approximate; this deep past is known mainly through archaeology.
Arawakan-speaking peoples, ancestors of the Taino, develop the farming, fishing and zemi-centered spiritual world that will define the island for centuries.
By this era the island is organized into five chiefdoms — Marien, Magua, Maguana, Higuey and Xaragua — each led by a cacique counseled by behiques, keepers of the zemi.
The southwestern kingdom of Xaragua, led by Bohechio with his sister Anacaona — poet and composer of areitos — is remembered as the center of Taino art and diplomacy.

Columbus lands near Môle-Saint-Nicolas and names the island La Isla Española. Weeks later, timbers from the wrecked Santa Maria become La Navidad — the first European settlement in the Americas, built on Taino land.
Returning on his second voyage, Columbus finds La Navidad burned and its garrison dead after clashes with the Taino — the first act of armed resistance to European settlement in the hemisphere.
Bartholomew Columbus founds Santo Domingo on the island's east — the base from which Spain will rule, and ruin, Ayiti.
Governor Ovando's fleet brings the first enslaved Africans to Hispaniola, opening four centuries of African bondage — and African resistance — in the Americas.
Invited to a feast of friendship, Xaragua's leaders are burned alive on Ovando's orders, and Queen Anacaona is hanged. Her name endures in Haiti as a symbol of dignity and loss.

Smallpox arrives amid enslavement in mines and encomiendas. Within a generation, a population once counted in the hundreds of thousands collapses toward extinction — though Taino blood and words survive in the Haitian people.
The cacique Enriquillo leads a fourteen-year guerrilla war from the Bahoruco mountains, forcing Spain to terms in 1533 — the first successful revolt against a European empire in the Americas.
Enslaved Africans on Diego Columbus's sugar estate rise up at Christmas — the first recorded African slave revolt in the New World. Maroon communities begin taking root in the mountains.
Spain forcibly empties the island's north and west to choke off contraband trade. The abandoned coasts become a vacuum — soon filled by buccaneers, and then by France.
French and English freebooters settle Île de la Tortue off the north coast — hunters, smugglers and pirates who become France's first foothold on the island.
Bertrand d'Ogeron becomes governor for the French crown, steering buccaneer camps toward a plantation colony.
The future Cap-Haïtien is founded and grows into the Paris of the Antilles — the commercial and cultural capital of the colony.
Louis XIV's slave code defines enslaved people as property while regulating baptism, punishment and manumission — the legal architecture of French slavery.
Spain formally cedes the island's western third to France. Saint-Domingue will become the richest colony on Earth — built on its deadliest slave system.
A new town is laid out on the Gulf of La Gonâve; it becomes the colonial capital in 1770, and Haiti's capital ever since.
The maroon leader Makandal organizes a clandestine network of poisonings and raids that terrifies the plantation regime for most of a decade.
Captured and burned alive at Cap-Français, Makandal passes into legend — many swore he escaped the flames in the form of a mosquito. His name endures in Vodou and in revolt.
A massive quake destroys the young capital, nineteen years after another shattered the north. Rebuilt low and in wood, the city keeps the scars.
More than 500 free men of color from Saint-Domingue — the Chasseurs-Volontaires — fight for American independence at the Siege of Savannah. Among them, tradition holds, a young Henry Christophe.

On the eve of revolution, Saint-Domingue produces roughly half the world's coffee and some forty percent of its sugar — wealth extracted from half a million enslaved people, tens of thousands of whom die each year.

Home from revolutionary Paris, the free man of color Vincent Ogé demands voting rights and raises an armed protest. Broken on the wheel in February 1791, he becomes a martyr whose execution radicalizes the colony.
At a nighttime Vodou ceremony, Dutty Boukman and the priestess Cécile Fatiman consecrate the coming uprising. Freedom, the prayer runs, speaks in every heart.
The enslaved people of the northern plain rise in coordinated revolt, burning a thousand plantations within weeks. The largest slave revolution in human history has begun.

events.t: Rights for free people of color
events.b: Paris grants full citizenship to free people of color, hoping to stabilize the colony — too late, and not nearly enough.
With Cap-Français in ashes from civil war, commissioner Sonthonax proclaims emancipation in the north — the same day Toussaint issues his own call to liberty at Camp Turel.
The National Convention abolishes slavery in all French colonies, ratifying what the revolution had already won on the ground. Toussaint Louverture rallies to the Republic.
After five years and catastrophic losses, Britain's invasion force evacuates. Toussaint — now the colony's dominant general — negotiates their exit himself.
The rivalry between Toussaint and André Rigaud erupts into civil war between north and south; Dessalines and Pétion serve on opposite sides.

Having taken Spanish Santo Domingo and abolished slavery across the whole island, Toussaint promulgates a constitution naming himself governor-for-life — autonomy in all but name, and a challenge Napoleon will not ignore.
Toussaint's adopted nephew Moyse takes the side of cultivators protesting the militarized plantation regime. His execution buys order at a heavy price in the people's trust.
Napoleon sends his brother-in-law Leclerc with what will grow to more than 40,000 troops — the largest expedition ever to leave France — to restore control, and in time, slavery.
Dessalines' outnumbered garrison holds the little fort for twenty days and bleeds the French army white. Marie-Jeanne Lamartinière fights on the ramparts, rifle in hand.

Lured to a conference and seized, Toussaint is deported to France. His warning survives him: in overthrowing me you have cut down only the trunk of the tree of liberty — it will spring back from the roots, for they are numerous and deep.

As news spreads that France has restored slavery in Guadeloupe, Pétion, Clervaux and Christophe abandon the French side. Sanité Bélair faces the firing squad refusing a blindfold. The war becomes a war of independence.

events.t: Toussaint dies at Fort de Joux
events.b: Starved and freezing in a cell in the Jura mountains, Toussaint Louverture dies on April 7 — ten months before the independence he made inevitable.
At the Congress of Arcahaie, Dessalines tears the white band from the French tricolor, and Catherine Flon sews blue to red — the flag of a nation about to be born.
Outside Cap, the Armée Indigène under Dessalines — with François Capois charging through cannon fire — breaks Rochambeau's army. It is the last great battle: France capitulates.
At Gonaïves, Dessalines proclaims independence and restores the island's Taino name: Ayiti. The first Black republic — the only nation ever born of a successful revolution of the enslaved.

On Dessalines' orders, most remaining French colonists are executed in the spring of 1804 — an act historians still debate, born of fourteen years of atrocity and the very real fear of slavery's return.
Dessalines is crowned Emperor of Haiti — a founder-emperor for a nation surrounded on every side by slaveholding empires that refuse to recognize it.
Work begins on Citadelle Laferrière, the mountaintop fortress built so that re-enslavement would be impossible. Twenty thousand laborers; walls four meters thick; never taken.
The imperial constitution abolishes slavery forever, bars foreign land ownership, and declares all Haitians — whatever their shade — black: citizenship defined by freedom, not color.
Ambushed at Pont-Rouge by his own officers, the founder is killed and mutilated; a poor woman remembered as Défilée gathers his remains. Haiti's original political wound.
The country splits: Christophe rules a State — soon a Kingdom — in the north, while Pétion leads a Republic in the south. Thirteen years of cold war between two visions of Haiti.
Christophe crowns himself king, creates a nobility of dukes and barons, and drives a literate, prosperous — and coerced — northern economy.
The palace at Milot — the Versailles of the Caribbean — stands finished: proof, Christophe insists, of what free Black civilization can build. A UNESCO World Heritage site since 1982.
Twice, Pétion shelters and re-arms Simón Bolívar — ships, muskets, men — asking one price: abolish slavery in the lands you free. Haiti midwifes Latin American independence.
Pétion dies beloved and nearly bankrupt; his secretary Jean-Pierre Boyer inherits the south — and, within four years, everything else.
Paralyzed by a stroke and facing mutiny, King Henry dies by his own hand — legend says with a silver bullet. His kingdom dissolves into Boyer's republic within weeks.
Boyer marches east and unifies the island, abolishing slavery in Santo Domingo. The union lasts twenty-two years; its memory shadows Haitian-Dominican relations still.

With warships offshore, Charles X grants recognition of independence for 150 million francs — compensation to the former enslavers. The double debt will drain Haiti for over a century, and shadows it still.
Boyer's Code Rural tries to bind cultivators to plantations to pay the debt. Rural Haiti answers by deepening its own counter-world: the lakou, the provision ground, the market woman.
France trims the indemnity to 90 million francs — still crushing, and now financed through French bank loans at interest. Haiti pays for its freedom twice.
An earthquake kills thousands and levels the great city of the north, Sans-Souci with it. The Cap never fully regains its old splendor.
After twenty-five years, the liberal revolution of Praslin ends Boyer's rule; a year later the east separates to become the Dominican Republic. Haiti's long century of turbulence begins.
In the south, Jean-Jacques Acaau and his peasant piquets — the army of the suffering — demand land and rights for the Black poor: rural Haiti announcing itself as a political force.
After a vision of the Virgin — Èzili Dantò to many — near the falls, Saut-d'Eau becomes Haiti's great pilgrimage: Catholic and Vodou devotion sharing a single waterfall each July.
President Faustin Soulouque crowns himself Emperor Faustin I, complete with an imperial court. European cartoonists mock; Haitian statecraft under permanent siege rarely gets read straight.
General Fabre Geffrard topples the Empire, restores the republic, and courts the Church and foreign respectability.
Haiti and the Vatican end a fifty-six-year schism; French clergy come to staff Haitian schools. A francophone elite culture deepens — and so does the distance from the Kreyòl-speaking majority.
Fifty-eight years after 1804, Lincoln's United States recognizes Haiti — slaveholding senators had blocked recognition for decades.
The Haitian anthropologist Anténor Firmin publishes De l'égalité des races humaines in Paris, dismantling scientific racism decades before the discipline caught up with him.
Port-au-Prince inaugurates its cast-iron market hall, ordered from Paris under President Hyppolite — soon the humming heart of the capital's commerce, run above all by its madan sara market women.
Pressured to lease a naval station, Haiti says no to the United States — Anténor Firmin holding the line opposite U.S. minister Frederick Douglass, who privately sympathized with the refusal.
Rather than surrender his flagship to a German gunboat, Admiral Hammerton Killick sends his crew ashore and blows up the Crête-à-Pierrot with himself aboard.
Haiti's national bank is reorganized under foreign — increasingly American — control. Fiscal sovereignty slips away before a single Marine has landed.
U.S. Marines walk into the Banque Nationale and remove half a million dollars of Haiti's gold reserve to New York for safekeeping. The occupation has a prologue.
Hours after President Vilbrun Guillaume Sam is killed by a Port-au-Prince crowd, U.S. forces seize the capital. The occupation will last nineteen years.
The Haitian-American Convention hands customs, finances and a new U.S.-officered Gendarmerie to American control.
A U.S.-drafted constitution opens Haitian land to foreign ownership, and forced road labor — the corvée — drives peasants into the Caco insurgency.
The Caco leader who vowed to drive the invaders into the sea is betrayed and shot. The Marines photograph his body lashed to a door — and hand the resistance its icon.
Benoît Batraville falls in turn; the pacification has killed thousands of Haitians. Resistance moves from the hills to the pen — to the students, the press, the poets.
Jean Price-Mars names the elite's collective bovarysme and tells Haiti that its folk culture — Kreyòl, Vodou, the lakou — is a civilization. Indigénisme is born.
Marines fire on protesting peasants near Les Cayes; strikes spread across the country. Washington begins planning its exit.
The last Marines embark and the Haitian flag rises alone again. American fiscal control, though, runs on until the debt's final payment.
On Trujillo's orders, Dominican soldiers slaughter Haitian families along the border — thousands upon thousands, killed with machetes to hide the state's hand. Haiti remembers it as Kout Kouto-a.

events.t: The Centre d'Art — and the peasant novel
events.b: A small Port-au-Prince art center opens; within years Hector Hyppolite and Philomé Obin hang in the world's museums. The same year, Jacques Roumain's Gouverneurs de la rosée gives Haitian literature its masterpiece.
Student strikes topple the old order, and Dumarsais Estimé becomes the first Black president since the occupation — labor laws, schools, and the noiriste politics that will outlive him.
Haiti retires the last loans descended from the 1825 indemnity — one hundred twenty-two years of paying for its own freedom, finally over. The development it purchased for France remains unrefunded.
For Port-au-Prince's two-hundredth birthday, Estimé builds a gleaming waterfront fairground — the Caribbean's own world's fair. The Cité de l'Exposition still frames the capital's seafront.
Hazel shreds the southern peninsula, killing perhaps a thousand people and gutting the coffee and cacao economy — and President Magloire's fortunes with it.
Saxophonist Nemours Jean-Baptiste debuts his konpa dirèk — the steady méringue groove that becomes Haiti's signature dance music, from Port-au-Prince to every diaspora dancefloor on Earth.
The country doctor François Duvalier wins an army-run election promising Black power and order. Haiti gets the most durable dictatorship in its history.
Duvalier builds a militia answerable to him alone — denim uniforms, dark glasses, machetes: the Volontaires de la Sécurité Nationale, named for the bogeyman who carries children off in a sack.

A referendum — official tally 2.8 million to 3,234 — makes Duvalier president-for-life. That summer the young exiles of Jeune Haïti land at Jérémie and are hunted down; the reprisals kill whole families.
Papa Doc dies in his bed; power passes to his son Jean-Claude, nineteen years old, with the machinery of fear intact.
Jean Dominique's Radio Haïti-Inter puts news, analysis and peasant voices on the air in Kreyòl — journalism the whole country can hear. The station will pay for it in blood.

Haiti reaches the World Cup — and for one immortal minute in Munich, Manno Sanon runs past Dino Zoff and scores on an Italy unbeaten in two years. Every Haitian of that generation knows where they were.
Young musicians fuse Vodou drums and rara horns with rock and reggae. Boukman Eksperyans and the roots movement turn ceremony into anthem — and, by Carnival 1990, into open protest.
Fearing swine fever, a U.S.-led program eradicates the kochon kreyòl — the peasant bank account on four legs. Rural Haiti's economy never quite recovers; neither does trust in outside help.
John Paul II, from the airport tarmac: things must change here. The ti legliz base communities take the Pope at his word.
Soldiers kill three schoolboys in Gonaïves — remembered as the three flowers of hope. The uprising that follows cannot be shot away.
A U.S. plane carries Baby Doc to France, ending twenty-nine years of family rule. In the streets: dechoukaj — the uprooting. February 7 becomes Haiti's democratic new year.
Overwhelmingly approved, it makes Kreyòl co-official with French, decentralizes power, and outlaws the old machinery of terror. Living up to it is another story.
Army-linked gunmen murder voters at the Ruelle Vaillant polling station and the election is annulled. Democracy's first attempt bleeds out in a schoolyard.
The slum priest of the ti legliz movement wins two-thirds of the vote in Haiti's first free election — the flood, Lavalas, of the poor into politics.
General Cédras' junta overthrows Aristide after seven months. Three years of terror follow: thousands killed, the FRAPH death squads, and botpippel dying at sea in flight.
With a U.S.-led force landing unopposed, the junta yields; Aristide returns in October preaching reconciliation over revenge.
Breath, Eyes, Memory announces a major writer telling Haiti's stories in English; Krik? Krak! follows within a year. The diaspora's voice joins the world's bookshelves.
Aristide disbands the Forces Armées d'Haïti — coup-maker of the century — trading soldiers for a new civilian National Police.
Aristide passes the sash to René Préval — the first time in one hundred ninety-two years that one elected Haitian president peacefully succeeds another.
The Fugees' album The Score goes diamond, and Wyclef Jean carries the Haitian flag onto the world's biggest stages. Sak pase becomes globally pronounceable.
Haiti's most fearless journalist is shot dead in Radio Haïti's courtyard. The crime, like too many others, is never solved; the station eventually falls silent.
Aristide wins again amid an opposition boycott and a poisoned dispute over how Senate seats were counted. Aid freezes; positions harden.
A presidential decree recognizes Vodou as a religion — its weddings and baptisms legal at last. Two centuries after Bois Caïman, the ancestors' practice steps out of hiding.
Aristide's government bills France 21,685,135,571 dollars and 48 cents — the 1825 ransom, computed with interest. Paris is not amused. The claim refuses to die.

In independence's two-hundredth year, armed revolt reaches the capital and Aristide leaves on a U.S. plane — a kidnapping, he says; a resignation, says Washington. U.N. troops arrive for a thirteen-year stay.
Tropical Storm Jeanne's floods kill some three thousand people in Gonaïves — deforested hills turning rain into rivers of mud.
Born in Port-au-Prince, a refugee of the Duvalier years, Michaëlle Jean becomes Governor General of Canada — the diaspora at the summit of a G7 state.
Fay, Gustav, Hanna and Ike strike within a single month; Gonaïves floods again and nearly eight hundred die — months after food-price riots showed how thin the margin already was.

At 4:53 in the afternoon, a magnitude-7.0 earthquake razes Port-au-Prince and its region. The dead are counted in the hundreds of thousands — estimates run from 100,000 to 316,000 — the state's own house collapsing with its people.
Cholera — traced to waste from a U.N. base — spreads down the Artibonite, ultimately killing nearly ten thousand people. The U.N. acknowledges its role only in 2016.
In a single year: Baby Doc flies home unpunished, Aristide returns from exile, and konpa star Michel Sweet Micky Martelly is sworn in as president.
Dany Laferrière — Port-au-Prince born, exiled under Duvalier — is elected to the Académie française: the first Haitian, and the first Québécois, under the Coupole.
A Category 4 landfall devastates the Grand'Anse and the Sud — hundreds dead, gardens and fruit trees stripped to the root, cholera resurgent in the ruins.
Fuel-price riots become a movement when the petrochallengers ask a single question — where did the PetroCaribe billions go? Audits name names; no one is convicted.
Months of country-on-lock: barricades, shuttered schools, a paralyzed economy — mass protest demanding President Moïse's resignation.
Gunmen kill President Jovenel Moïse in his own bedroom. The plot's full authorship remains unresolved; the state's unraveling accelerates.

A magnitude-7.2 quake kills more than two thousand two hundred people in the southern peninsula; days later a storm soaks the ruins. Aid moves slower than in 2010 — the roads now belong to armed groups.

events.t: The world votes to help — again
events.b: The U.N. Security Council authorizes a Kenya-led Multinational Security Support mission against the gangs — the fourth international intervention in thirty years.

With the capital besieged and the prime minister locked out of the country, a nine-member Transitional Presidential Council takes office to steer toward elections; Kenyan police land in June. The story continues.
